newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada moves to counter U.S. law on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Canada moves to counter U.S. law on Cuba.

text.p: The Canadian government said on Friday it would introduce a bill on Monday to counter hotly debated U.S. legislation that penalizes some foreign companies that invest in Cuba.

The government has used every opportunity to rail against the Helms-Burton Act, which it says illegitimately tries to extend U.S. law to third countries, and had previously said it would introduce counter-legislation.

The bill, which would amend the Foreign Extraterritorial Measures Act, will be submitted to the House of Commons -- Parliament's lower chamber -- on Monday, the first day of business after a summer break.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and International Trade said on Friday the legislation would "contain important measures to counter the effects on Canadian companies of ... the Helms-Burton Act."

The government said earlier the bill would allow Canadians to counter-sue in Canadian courts to recover damages awarded by U.S. courts. It would also allow Canada's attorney-general to issue blocking orders declaring that judgments handed down under any objectionable foreign law would not be enforced or recognized in Canada.

Helms-Burton provides for U.S. companies and citizens to sue foreign companies dealing with former American-owned properties in Cuba. Executives of these companies and their families can be banned from entering the United States.

President Bill Clinton has waived until at least early next year the provision for lawsuits but Canada has vowed to press ahead with its legislation to be ready for future U.S. moves. Canadian officials acknowledge whatever bill they put forward would not be able to block the U.S. law completely.
Ottawa is also considering challenging Helms-Burton under the North American Free Trade Agreement, which groups the United States, Canada and Mexico.
